title: Ἀνὴρ κομπαστής
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 51 (= Perry 33). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἀνὴρ πένταθλος ἐπὶ ἀνανδρίᾳ ἑκάστοτε ὑπὸ τῶν πολιτῶν ὀνειδιζόμενος, ἀποδημήσας ποτὲ καὶ μετὰ χρόνον ἐπανελθών, ἀλαζονευόμενος ἔλεγεν ὡς πολλὰ καὶ ἐν ἄλλαις πόλεσιν ἀνδραγαθήσας, ἐν τῇ Ρόδῳ τοιοῦτον ἥλατο πήδημα ὡς μηδένα τῶν Ὀλυμπιονικῶν ἐφικέσθαι· καὶ τούτου μάρτυρας ἔφασκε παρέξεσθαι τοὺς παρατετυχηκότας, ἂν ἄρα ποτὲ ἐπιδημήσωσι.
sentences.tr: Anēr pentathlos epi anandriai hekastote hypo tōn politōn oneidizomenos, apodēmēsas pote kai meta chronon epanelthōn, alazoneuomenos elegen hōs polla kai en allais polesin andragathēsas, en tēi Rhodōi toiouton hēlato pēdēma hōs mēdena tōn Olympionikōn ephikesthai· kai toutou martyras ephaske parexesthai tous paratetychēkotas, an ara pote epidēmēsōsi.
sentences.l: A pentathlete, reproached at every turn by his fellow citizens for unmanliness, having once gone abroad and after a time come back, boasting used to say that, having done many brave deeds in other cities as well, in Rhodes he leaped such a leap as none of the Olympic victors had reached; and he kept saying that he would produce as witnesses of this the men who had been present, if ever they should come to town.
sentences.i: A pentathlete whom his fellow citizens were forever taunting with cowardice went abroad, and when after a time he came home he boasted that he had performed many feats in other cities, and that in Rhodes he had made such a jump as no Olympic victor had ever matched; and he kept saying he would produce as witnesses the men who had been there, if ever they should visit.
sentences.n: ἀνανδρία is failure of manly courage, a heavy charge against an athlete. The pentathlon included the long jump, which is why the boast takes this shape. ὡς … ἐφικέσθαι is a result clause with the infinitive, 'such a jump that none reached it'. ἄν (for ἐάν) with the subjunctive ἐπιδημήσωσι leaves the condition open — the witnesses are conveniently elsewhere.

sentences.t: Τῶν δὲ παρόντων τις ὑποτυχὼν ἔφη πρὸς αὐτόν· « Ἀλλ’, ὦ οὗτος, εἰ τοῦτο ἀληθές ἐστι, οὐδὲν δεῖ σοι μαρτύρων· αὐτοῦ γὰρ καὶ Ῥόδος καὶ πήδημα. »
sentences.tr: Tōn de parontōn tis hypotychōn ephē pros auton· « All’, ō houtos, ei touto alēthes esti, ouden dei soi martyrōn· autou gar kai Rhodos kai pēdēma. »
sentences.l: And one of those present, taking him up, said to him: « But, you there, if this is true, you have no need of witnesses: for here is Rhodes and here is the jump. »
sentences.n: αὐτοῦ is the adverb 'right here, on this spot', not the pronoun 'of him' — the two are written alike apart from the breathing. δεῖ takes the genitive of the thing needed (μαρτύρων) and a dative of the person needing. ὑποτυχών, 'having caught him up', is the regular word for breaking into another's speech. This is the fable behind the Latin tag hic Rhodus, hic salta.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι ὧν πρόχειρος ἡ δι’ ἔργων πεῖρα, περὶ τούτων πᾶς λόγος περιττός ἐστι.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti hōn procheiros hē di’ ergōn peira, peri toutōn pas logos perittos esti.
sentences.l: The story shows that of those things of which the test by deeds is ready to hand, about these every word is superfluous.
sentences.i: The story shows that where a thing can be put to the proof in deed, all talk about it is superfluous.
sentences.n: ὧν … περὶ τούτων: the relative comes first and the demonstrative picks it up afterwards — a very Greek way of building a sentence, where English would put the main clause first.
